title: A Life of Philip K. Dick: The Man Who Remembered the Future
author: Anthony Peake

page_summary:
Anthony Peake's A Life of Philip K. Dick: The Man Who Remembered the Future (Arcturus Publishing, 2013) is the most recent comprehensive English-language biography and the one most willing to take PKD's anomalous-cognition claims seriously as candidate veridical experience. Peake comes to PKD from a parallel career as a popular consciousness-studies author (Is There Life After Death?, 2006; The Daemon, 2008; The Out-of-Body Experience, 2011; Cheating the Ferryman, 2019, and others), and his Dick biography is an outgrowth of that broader project rather than an isolated act of literary biography.

Method and frame: Where Sutin records and Arnold psychologizes, Peake entertains the hypothesis that PKD's visions registered something real about consciousness, time, and the structure of reality. The methodological frame is therefore more permissive than the academic biographies — Peake reads PKD's claims of precognition, of accessing information beyond normal sensory channels, and of receiving transmissions from non-local sources as candidates for a kind of cognitive event consciousness studies has been trying to characterize. The book has been received cautiously in academic Dick studies for that reason; readers who want neutral or skeptical biography prefer Sutin or Rickman. But the comprehensive coverage of the life is genuine — at 448 pages it is comparable in scope to Sutin — and Peake's openness to the visionary content makes the book unusually attentive to material the more skeptical biographies treat in passing.

Contributions to PKD studies: (1) the most permissive biographical frame for the 2-3-74 visions, treating them as candidate veridical anomalous cognition rather than reflexively as pathology or as literary frame; (2) comprehensive coverage of the life with the post-1974 period given full biographical weight (where Sutin's account compresses some late material); (3) connection of PKD to the broader parapsychology and consciousness-studies literatures Peake works in elsewhere — a context most academic biographies omit; (4) an explicit counter-frame to Arnold's clinical-psychological reading, useful for triangulation; (5) updated post-2011-Exegesis biographical synthesis (Peake has access to the Lethem/Jackson edition that Sutin did not).

Position in the literature: Peake stands in deliberate contrast to Kyle Arnold's The Divine Madness of PKD (2016) — the two biographies appeared within three years of each other and represent the two principal post-Sutin frames for the visionary material. Lawrence Sutin's Divine Invasions (1989) remains the source-of-record on biographical events and dates; Peake's project is to extend Sutin's coverage and to redirect the interpretive frame for the late period. Anne Dick's The Search for PKD (1995/2010) and Rickman's interview-volumes give first-person witness material that all comprehensive biographies depend on; Peake works from those sources as well as his own.

Fan reception: Peake is widely read in fan venues, including Total Dick-Head, PKD Otaku, and the Daniel Pinchbeck-adjacent psychedelic-spiritual lineage of writing on Dick. Some academic readers are less convinced by the parapsychological frame, but the book's biographical thoroughness has earned respect even from those who reject the interpretive frame. Erik Davis's High Weirdness (2019) shares part of the frame and is the academically credentialed parallel.

Caveats: The frame is methodologically permissive in a way some academic readers find untenable — Peake's willingness to take precognition and non-local cognition as live possibilities reflects his broader career and is not a position the academic Dick literature has consensus on. Pair with Arnold (2016) for the clinical counter-frame and with Sutin (1989) for the reportorial baseline.
